newsitem.title: UK: Hambros says CWS debacle will hit business.
newsitem.headline: Hambros says CWS debacle will hit business.

text.p: British investment bank Hambros said on Wednesday its climbdown over supporting Andrew Regan in his failed take-over bid for the Co-operative Wholesale Society (CWS) would have an impact on new business.

"My own view is it will have an impact but it will not be long-lived...the impact will be fairly modest," Michael Sorkin, deputy chairman of Hambros Bank told Reuters after reporting annual pre-tax profits of 64.7 million pounds ($106 million).
Earlier Hambros' chief executive Sir Chips Keswick said the group would take any action necessary as soon as possible to ensure the bank preserved and enhanced its reputation.

"We believe that this will enable us to put the matter behind us and continue the momentum of current business efforts in corporate finance and the rest of the bank," he said in Hambros' statement of its results for the year to March 31.
But Sorkin said the result of an independent probe by law firm Norton Rose into Hambros' role in the Co-op saga, would not be made public despite press speculation.

The group reported significantly improved pre-tax profits for 1996/97, up from 20.6 million the year before but said core banking returns were still inadequate. Hambros's shares were up 5.5 pence at 237.5 pence by the close of trading.

Finance director Simon Leathes said the banking group should achieve a return on capital of 15 percent compared with a current level of less than five percent. But the nature of the business made it difficult to set a target date for achieving this.
In April Hambros made an embarrassing unreserved apology for supporting Regan in his discredited 1.2 billion pound bid for mutually-owned supermarkets-to-funeral parlours group CWS.
It also made a significant financial settlement with CWS, believed by banking sources to be in the region of a million pounds.

Hambros said it had provisioned for the costs of the CWS affair but Leathes would not say how much of a 9.0 million pound exceptional charge was as a result of this expense, which related principally to implementing recent strategic reviews.
The liquidator of bidding vehicle Galileo was last month said to be considering suing the bank for the quality of advice it had given the offshoot of Guernsey-based investment trust Lanica.

Despite the CWS debacle and the adverse publicity which accompanied it, Hambros said it expects steady improvement from its banking group, as the benefits of a strategic review would take time to flow through.

"Although the return on capital earned by the banking group...was still inadequate, we have made progress towards our medium term objectives in each main area of activity," Hambros' chief executive Sir Chips Keswick said in its results statement.
Keswick said the prospects for Hambro Countrywide, the estate agency business in which Hambros has a majority shareholding, were excellent.
He also expects progressive, steady improvement for the banking group, an important contribution from Hambros' investment group and further underlying growth from Hambros Insurance Services.
Keswick said the group remained committed to ensuring the capital employed in its banking business earned "satisfactory and sustainable" returns for shareholders.
"We intend to make steady and progressive improvements to this end," Keswick said.

The group expects a modest first year contribution from its merged Guinness Flight Hambro Asset Management business due to the initial costs of reorganisation then "a useful and growing contribution".
"We will seek further to reduce costs across the rest of the banking group," Keswick said.
Earnings per share for the group were 12.5 pence against a 7.6 pence loss the previous year while the total dividend was unchanged at 7.5 pence. ($ = 0.610 British Pounds)
